one_liner: Student C11 Linux file-copy tool with threaded pipeline and io_uring backends, compared only against its own naive read/write loop.
what_it_does: A cp-like CLI (copyfast [OPTIONS] SRC DST) that copies files or directory trees with a selectable engine (naive, pipeline, uring), optional SHA-256 or xxHash64 verification, sparse-hole preservation, metadata preservation and a resumable CRC32-checked journal. There is no library API: the backends are internal functions behind copy_file_dispatch(). It is not command-line compatible with GNU cp.
how_it_is_fast: The pipeline backend runs a reader pthread (pread) and a writer pthread (pwrite) over a bounded pool of 4 KB-aligned 1 MB slots, so reads and writes overlap. The io_uring backend submits up to queue_depth reads via liburing and chains a write SQE on each read completion. Directory copies use a bounded work queue drained by -j N worker threads. Sparse files are walked with lseek(SEEK_HOLE/SEEK_DATA) and holes are skipped. It does not use copy_file_range, sendfile or reflinks (FICLONE), which are what make modern cp fast.
when_to_use: Reading a compact, readable example of a reader/writer bounded-buffer copy pipeline in C11 with pthreads
Studying a minimal liburing read-then-write copy loop with fixed slot buffers
Teaching SEEK_HOLE/SEEK_DATA sparse copying and a resume journal design
Linux-only experiments on page-cache-resident files where you want to compare overlap strategies yourself
when_not_to_use: As a production replacement for GNU cp, rsync, fcp or wcp: no license, 7 commits, 0 stars, and it was never benchmarked against cp
On filesystems where cp would reflink or use copy_file_range (Btrfs, XFS, NFS server-side copy): copyfast always moves bytes through user space
When you need durability: no backend fsyncs the destination unless -v or an interrupt triggers fdatasync, so timings and 'done' mean data is only in the page cache
Non-Linux platforms: requires liburing and Linux syscalls
Trees of many small files with -j 1: each file takes the pipeline path, which spawns two threads and allocates 8 x 1 MB buffers per file

integration.min_toolchain: C11 (GCC or Clang, -std=c11 -D_GNU_SOURCE); compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: Linux only (io_uring needs a 5.x+ kernel; README results on Linux 6.18 x86_64)
integration.thread_safety: not applicable as a library; internal stats use C11 atomics, and the work queue and buffer pool use mutex plus condition variables
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — a cp-style CLI with different flags (-R, -j, -b, -S, -p); not a GNU cp drop-in

gotchas: Multi-file benchmark confound: copy_file_dispatch sends files under 512 KB to the naive backend only when jobs > 1, so the -j 1 'baseline' copies each 32 KB file via the pipeline backend (two pthread_create calls plus 8 MB of posix_memalign per file) while -j 4/-j 8 use the naive loop. The 10.49x 4-worker figure therefore mixes a backend change with parallelism, which also explains why it is super-linear and why 8 workers (3.45x) is slower than 4.

The io_uring backend ignores short writes (a completion with res smaller than the requested length is counted and the slot freed with no resubmission), and its SQ-full fallback discards the pwrite return value, so a partial write could silently truncate data; none of this affects the published numbers on a local filesystem but it is a correctness gap.

bench/benchmark.c times one run per backend, in a fixed order, on a 100 MB file just written to /tmp and still page-cache resident, with no destination fsync; results measure memory-to-page-cache copy, not NVMe throughput (and /tmp may be tmpfs). The dense test also runs with sparse_aware=true.
posix_fadvise is called with POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL | POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED; these are enum values, not flags, so the OR evaluates to WILLNEED only.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only for reading the code: for real copies prefer fcp or wcp (both measured against GNU cp, the latter with an io_uring design) or uring-sync for many small files, all of which beat cp itself rather than a self-written naive loop.
verified_claims_summary: The README's single-run table, produced by bench/benchmark.c and bench/run_benchmarks.sh, shows a 100 MB page-cache-resident file copied in 0.0376 s by the threaded pipeline vs 0.0869 s by the project's own sequential read/write loop (2.31x) and 0.0487 s by io_uring, on Linux 6.18 x86_64 with -O3 and an unstated CPU and compiler; GNU cp was never measured. The 1,000-file 10.49x figure compares 4 workers on the naive path against 1 worker on the heavier per-file pipeline path, so it is not a clean parallelism measurement.
status_note: Seven-commit OS-course project (Week 12 viva checklist, syllabus matrix) last updated 2026-10-04 with no license file, so it is reference-only and cannot legally be copied.
